slides.direction: The root-cause box of section 2.13, one line at a time.
slides.text:
Observed behavior : git update-ref main <id> prints nothing. Afterwards "main" is ambiguous and
                    resolves to <id>, while the branch main still points at its own commit.
Git state         : a file .git/main holds <id>. refs/heads/main is unchanged. git for-each-ref,
                    which lists refs/, does not show the stray ref.
Mechanism         : update-ref writes exactly the ref it is given. For an update it checks only
                    that the name is well-formed. Name lookup tries <name> at the top of .git
                    before refs/heads/<name>. For a deletion Git accepts only names under refs/
                    and names in capitals such as ORIG_HEAD, so "git update-ref -d main" is refused.
Root cause        : a plumbing command received a short name where it needs the full ref name.
Why Git does this : plumbing serves scripts. It does what it is told and guesses nothing.
Correct fix       : confirm that .git/main is the stray ref, then delete that file.
Prevention        : write refs/heads/<name> for update-ref; move branches with porcelain.
slides.caption: The mechanism: update-ref writes exactly the ref it is given, and for an update it checks only that the name is well-formed.

items: Thinking a branch contains commits. Root cause: a branch is a ref that names one commit; "its commits" are whatever is reachable from there.
Believing that deleting a branch deletes commits. Root cause: deleting a branch deletes a name; unreachable objects remain until garbage collection, after a grace period.
Reading HEAD as "the latest commit". Root cause: HEAD is a symbolic ref to the current branch, or a direct reference to a commit, in which case no branch is current.
A name such as main is reported ambiguous. Root cause: a stray ref outside refs/, written by git update-ref with a short name.
Answering "which commit is deployed?" with a branch name. Root cause: main is a moving name; it meant another commit yesterday and may mean a different one in a colleague's clone today.

beats.text: A customer reports a bug that you fixed last week. Your CTO asks one calm question: "Is the fix in what we shipped?"
beats.tele: A customer reports a bug that you fixed last week. Your CTO asks one calm question: "Is the fix in what we shipped?"

beats.text: You could open the release notes. You could search the log for the message. Both can mislead you, because a message can appear on a commit that isn't in the release. So how would you know for certain?
beats.tele: You could open the release notes. You could search the log for the message. Both can mislead you, because a message can appear on a commit that isn't in the release. So how would you know for certain?

beats.text: The question is an ancestry question, and Git answers it with an exit status, the number a command reports when it finishes: is the fix commit reachable from the released commit, yes or no. To ask it, you need to know what "reachable" means, and what a name such as main really is. That's this video.
beats.tele: The question is an ancestry question, and Git answers it with an exit status, the number a command reports when it finishes: is the fix commit reachable from the released commit, yes or no. To ask it, you need to know what "reachable" means, and what a name such as `main` really is. That's this video.

beats.text: The commit graph. In one sentence: every commit names its parent commits, so the commits form a graph that is walked from child to parent, and "the history of X" means everything you can reach from X by following those links.
beats.tele: The commit graph. In one sentence: every commit names its parent commits, so the commits form a graph that is walked from child to parent, and "the history of X" means everything you can reach from X by following those links.

beats.text: Now precisely. The commits form a directed acyclic graph, a DAG. It's directed because the link is stored in the child and points at the parent. It's acyclic because a commit's ID is computed from its parents' IDs: a parent must exist before its child, so no chain of links can return to its start.
beats.tele: Now precisely. The commits form a directed acyclic graph, a DAG. It's directed because the link is stored in the child and points at the parent. It's acyclic because a commit's ID is computed from its parents' IDs: a parent must exist before its child, so no chain of links can return to its start.

beats.text: An object is reachable from another if a chain leads to it that follows tags to what they tag, commits to their parents and trees, and trees to their entries. If that felt fast, here it is in one sentence: reachable means you can get there by following links.
beats.tele: An object is reachable from another if a chain leads to it that follows tags to what they tag, commits to their parents and trees, and trees to their entries. If that felt fast, here it is in one sentence: reachable means you can get there by following links.

beats.text: Three things follow, and each corrects a common belief.
beats.tele: Three things follow, and each corrects a common belief.

beats.text: One: a commit doesn't know its children. So "what came after this commit?" has an answer only relative to a starting point. History commands start from a ref, a name that points at a commit, like the labels now on screen.
beats.tele: One: a commit doesn't know its children. So "what came after this commit?" has an answer only relative to a starting point. History commands start from a ref, a name that points at a commit, like the labels now on screen.

beats.text: Two: "the commits on a branch" is not a stored list. It's the set reachable from the commit that the branch names.
beats.tele: Two: "the commits on a branch" is not a stored list. It's the set reachable from the commit that the branch names.

beats.text: Three: "A is an ancestor of B" means that A is reachable from B. git merge-base --is-ancestor A B answers with its exit status.
beats.tele: Three: "A is an ancestor of B" means that A is reachable from B. `git merge-base --is-ancestor A B` answers with its exit status.

beats.text: And inside the dot git folder, the graph isn't stored anywhere as a whole. Parent IDs are inside commit objects, and the starting points are refs.
beats.tele: And inside the dot git folder, the graph isn't stored anywhere as a whole. Parent IDs are inside commit objects, and the starting points are refs.

beats.text: Unreachable is not gone. A commit that no ref reaches still exists as an object. Deleting a branch deletes a name, never a commit. git gc, Git's garbage collection, removes unreachable objects only after a grace period, two weeks by default. The setting is gc.pruneExpire. Reflog entries also count as starting points. A reflog is the local journal of where a ref has pointed.
beats.tele: Unreachable is not gone. A commit that no ref reaches still exists as an object. Deleting a branch deletes a name, never a commit. `git gc`, Git's garbage collection, removes unreachable objects only after a grace period, two weeks by default. The setting is `gc.pruneExpire`. Reflog entries also count as starting points. A reflog is the local journal of where a ref has pointed.

beats.text: Its entries are kept for 90 days by default, or 30 days once the commit is no longer reachable from the tip of its ref. The settings are gc.reflogExpire and gc.reflogExpireUnreachable. The lab configuration sets both of those to never, as video 1 explained. The recovery chapter is built on these numbers.

beats.text: refs/heads/<name> is a branch. It refers to a commit, and it moves when you commit, merge, reset or rebase while it is the current branch.
beats.tele: `refs/heads/<name>` is a branch. It refers to a commit, and it moves when you commit, merge, reset or rebase while it is the current branch.

beats.text: refs/tags/<name> is a tag. It refers usually to a commit or a tag object, and it normally never moves.
beats.tele: `refs/tags/<name>` is a tag. It refers usually to a commit or a tag object, and it normally never moves.

beats.text: refs/remotes/<remote>/<name> is a remote-tracking branch. It refers to a commit, and it moves when you fetch from that remote or push to it.
beats.tele: `refs/remotes/<remote>/<name>` is a remote-tracking branch. It refers to a commit, and it moves when you fetch from that remote or push to it.

beats.text: HEAD refers to the current branch, as a symbolic ref, or to one commit ID directly, which is called detached HEAD. It moves when you switch.
beats.tele: `HEAD` refers to the current branch, as a symbolic ref, or to one commit ID directly, which is called detached HEAD. It moves when you switch.

beats.text: A branch contains no commits. It names one, and its history is what is reachable from there. Creating a branch writes one ref and copies nothing. And Git records no "parent branch", so merge and rebase must be told the other side.

beats.text: A caution about files. In this video each ref is a file that cat can read. That's the default "files" format, not a guarantee: refs can be packed into one file, and the reftable format stores them in binary. git rev-parse, git symbolic-ref and git for-each-ref work with every format.

beats.text: Risk labels. git branch <name> is 🟢 SAFE: it adds one ref. git switch is 🟢 SAFE: it changes HEAD, the index and the working tree, and refuses to overwrite uncommitted changes. git update-ref is 🟡 CAUTION: it changes one ref and nothing else.
beats.tele: Risk labels. `git branch <name>` is 🟢 SAFE: it adds one ref. `git switch` is 🟢 SAFE: it changes HEAD, the index and the working tree, and refuses to overwrite uncommitted changes. `git update-ref` is 🟡 CAUTION: it changes one ref and nothing else.

beats.text: For the graph, the textbook's analogy is a family tree in which each record lists the parents and none lists the children. From any person you can find all ancestors, but to find descendants you must start from someone younger. It breaks on the counts: a commit has no parent, which makes it a root commit. Or one parent, an ordinary commit. Or several, a merge.

Or one parent, an ordinary commit. Or several, a merge.

beats.text: For refs: sticky labels on a wall chart of the commit graph. Moving a label changes nothing on the chart, and removing one removes no commit. HEAD is the "you are here" marker, normally stuck onto a label rather than onto the chart. It breaks because labels are local: every clone has its own set, and learns about another repository's labels only when it fetches.

HEAD is the "you are here" marker, normally stuck onto a label rather than onto the chart. It breaks because labels are local: every clone has its own set, and learns about another repository's labels only when it fetches.

beats.text: Combine them. The chart is permanent and shared by content. The labels are small, movable and yours. Almost every Git command you'll learn moves labels.

beats.text: Time flows left to right. Two commits, then a fork: one commit on one line, one on the other. They join in 2511274, the merge, which has two parents. main points there, and HEAD names main. feature/dedupe points at ea0d3fa. The last commit on the right, 2c65cfc, is the one we'll create without a name and then rescue.
beats.tele: Time flows left to right. Two commits, then a fork: one commit on one line, one on the other. They join in `2511274`, the merge, which has two parents. `main` points there, and HEAD names `main`. `feature/dedupe` points at `ea0d3fa`. The last commit on the right, `2c65cfc`, is the one we'll create without a name and then rescue.

beats.text: Before: two labels on one commit, and HEAD attached to the label feature/unicode. After: a new commit whose parent is the old one. The label feature/unicode moved to it. main didn't move. HEAD didn't move either: it's still attached to the same label, and the label carried it.

beats.text: Five commits, one of them a merge.
beats.tele: Five commits, one of them a merge.

beats.text: Try it now. Before the next snippet, draw this graph on paper from the picture, with arrows from child to parent. Thirty seconds. Then check your answer against the parent pointers.
beats.tele: Try it now. Before the next snippet, draw this graph on paper from the picture, with arrows from child to parent. Thirty seconds. Then check your answer against the parent pointers.

beats.text: %p prints the parents. The merge commit 2511274 has two parent lines: first the commit that main pointed at when the merge was made, 6d7e946, then the tip of the merged branch, ea0d3fa. A merge commit is an ordinary commit with more than one parent, and its tree is the merged snapshot. The root, dec99b5, has none. Did your arrows point from old to new? Almost everyone draws them that way first. Git stores them the other way: each child points back at its parents.

beats.text: Predict: how many commits are reachable from main, and how many from feature/dedupe? Say it out loud. I'll wait.

beats.text: Five from main. Three from feature/dedupe: its own commit and the two it shares with main. And the ancestry test: the branch is an ancestor of main, status 0. main is not an ancestor of the branch, status 1. That's the command for "is the fix in what we shipped?". One line, and the CTO has an answer.

beats.text: Now a commit with no name. git commit-tree writes a commit object and moves no ref.
beats.tele: Now a commit with no name. `git commit-tree` writes a commit object and moves no ref.

beats.text: Stop here. A sixth commit was created, 2c65cfc, whose parent is the tip of main. Where is it now?
beats.tele: Stop here. A sixth commit was created, `2c65cfc`, whose parent is the tip of `main`. Where is it now?

beats.text: It's in the object database: git cat-file -t says commit. But git rev-list --count --all still counts five, and git fsck reports a dangling commit. It exists, and no ref leads to it.
beats.tele: It's in the object database: `git cat-file -t` says `commit`. But `git rev-list --count --all` still counts five, and `git fsck` reports a dangling commit. It exists, and no ref leads to it.

beats.text: git branch rescue <id> 🟢 SAFE created a ref for it. Six commits are reachable, git fsck is silent, and the graph shows the commit. No object changed. A name was added.
beats.tele: `git branch rescue <id>` 🟢 SAFE created a ref for it. Six commits are reachable, `git fsck` is silent, and the graph shows the commit. No object changed. A name was added.

beats.text: One commit on main. We read the ref files.
beats.tele: One commit on `main`. We read the ref files.

beats.text: HEAD contains the name of a branch, and the branch file contains a commit ID. git rev-parse resolves both names to that ID. git symbolic-ref HEAD prints the branch that HEAD names.
beats.tele: HEAD contains the name of a branch, and the branch file contains a commit ID. `git rev-parse` resolves both names to that ID. `git symbolic-ref HEAD` prints the branch that HEAD names.

beats.text: Quick quiz, three options. git branch feature/unicode creates a branch. How many objects does it add? Option one: none. Option two: one. Option three: a copy of every commit. Say it out loud.
beats.tele: Quick quiz, three options. `git branch feature/unicode` creates a branch. How many objects does it add? Option one: none. Option two: one. Option three: a copy of every commit. Say it out loud.

beats.text: Option one: none. The object list is identical before and after. The command wrote one small file holding one ID. git for-each-ref lists every ref with the object it names: two refs, one commit.
beats.tele: Option one: none. The object list is identical before and after. The command wrote one small file holding one ID. `git for-each-ref` lists every ref with the object it names: two refs, one commit.

beats.text: Now we switch and commit. Predict which of three files change: HEAD, refs/heads/main, refs/heads/feature/unicode.
beats.tele: Now we switch and commit. Predict which of three files change: `HEAD`, `refs/heads/main`, `refs/heads/feature/unicode`.

beats.text: git switch 🟢 SAFE rewrote HEAD to name the other branch. The commit then moved feature/unicode to 4a3fb80. main stayed at 3046dc6, and HEAD reads the same before and after the commit.
beats.tele: `git switch` 🟢 SAFE rewrote HEAD to name the other branch. The commit then moved `feature/unicode` to `4a3fb80`. `main` stayed at `3046dc6`, and HEAD reads the same before and after the commit.

beats.text: Here's that as a picture. A commit moves the current branch, and HEAD follows because it names that branch.
beats.tele: Here's that as a picture. A commit moves the current branch, and HEAD follows because it names that branch.

beats.text: Older scripts switch branches with git checkout. Same effect. You see it once here so that you can read those scripts.
beats.tele: Older scripts switch branches with `git checkout`. Same effect. You see it once here so that you can read those scripts.

beats.text: The second form of HEAD. git switch --detach wrote a commit ID into HEAD. git symbolic-ref fails, because HEAD isn't a symbolic ref now. No branch is current, so a new commit would move no branch. Switching back to main restores the symbolic form. Video 24 is devoted to this state.
beats.tele: The second form of HEAD. `git switch --detach` wrote a commit ID into HEAD. `git symbolic-ref` fails, because HEAD isn't a symbolic ref now. No branch is current, so a new commit would move no branch. Switching back to `main` restores the symbolic form. Video 24 is devoted to this state.

beats.text: The trap. The intent is to move the branch main to the first commit. The name given to git update-ref 🟡 CAUTION is main instead of refs/heads/main. Predict what moves.
beats.tele: The trap. The intent is to move the branch `main` to the first commit. The name given to `git update-ref` 🟡 CAUTION is `main` instead of `refs/heads/main`. Predict what moves.

beats.text: The command printed nothing, and the branch did not move: git branch -vv still shows cfa6dbc. But the name main now resolves to the old commit, with a warning that the name is ambiguous.
beats.tele: The command printed nothing, and the branch did not move: `git branch -vv` still shows `cfa6dbc`. But the name `main` now resolves to the old commit, with a warning that the name is ambiguous.

beats.text: git for-each-ref, which lists refs/, doesn't show the stray ref. A listing of the top of .git does: a file .git/main, holding the old ID. git update-ref -d main is refused, and the fix is to delete that file.
beats.tele: `git for-each-ref`, which lists `refs/`, doesn't show the stray ref. A listing of the top of `.git` does: a file `.git/main`, holding the old ID. `git update-ref -d main` is refused, and the fix is to delete that file.

beats.text: The mechanism: update-ref writes exactly the ref it is given, and for an update it checks only that the name is well-formed. Name lookup tries the name at the top of .git before refs/heads/. For a deletion, Git accepts only names under refs/ and names in capitals such as ORIG_HEAD.
beats.tele: The mechanism: `update-ref` writes exactly the ref it is given, and for an update it checks only that the name is well-formed. Name lookup tries the name at the top of `.git` before `refs/heads/`. For a deletion, Git accepts only names under `refs/` and names in capitals such as `ORIG_HEAD`.

beats.text: The root cause: a plumbing command received a short name where it needs the full ref name. Why Git does this: plumbing serves scripts. It does what it's told and guesses nothing. Prevention: write refs/heads/<name> for update-ref, and move branches with porcelain, the everyday commands.
beats.tele: The root cause: a plumbing command received a short name where it needs the full ref name. Why Git does this: plumbing serves scripts. It does what it's told and guesses nothing. Prevention: write `refs/heads/<name>` for `update-ref`, and move branches with porcelain, the everyday commands.

beats.text: The textbook notes that the two name checks were read from the Git 2.55.0 source, and that the fix applies to the files format, where a ref is a file.
beats.tele: The textbook notes that the two name checks were read from the Git 2.55.0 source, and that the fix applies to the files format, where a ref is a file.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Thinking a branch contains commits. Root cause: a branch is a ref that names one commit; "its commits" are whatever is reachable from there.
beats.tele: Thinking a branch contains commits. Root cause: a branch is a ref that names one commit; "its commits" are whatever is reachable from there.

beats.text: Believing that deleting a branch deletes commits. Root cause: deleting a branch deletes a name; unreachable objects remain until garbage collection, after a grace period.
beats.tele: Believing that deleting a branch deletes commits. Root cause: deleting a branch deletes a name; unreachable objects remain until garbage collection, after a grace period.

beats.text: Reading HEAD as "the latest commit". Root cause: HEAD is a symbolic ref to the current branch, or a direct reference to a commit, in which case no branch is current.
beats.tele: Reading HEAD as "the latest commit". Root cause: HEAD is a symbolic ref to the current branch, or a direct reference to a commit, in which case no branch is current.

beats.text: A name such as main is reported ambiguous. Root cause: a stray ref outside refs/, written by git update-ref with a short name.
beats.tele: A name such as `main` is reported ambiguous. Root cause: a stray ref outside `refs/`, written by `git update-ref` with a short name.

beats.text: Answering "which commit is deployed?" with a branch name. Root cause: main is a moving name; it meant another commit yesterday and may mean a different one in a colleague's clone today.
beats.tele: Answering "which commit is deployed?" with a branch name. Root cause: `main` is a moving name; it meant another commit yesterday and may mean a different one in a colleague's clone today.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. A backend team ships release builds from tagged commits. A fix for a retry bug is merged, and a customer on the previous release still sees the bug. "Is the fix in what we shipped?" is settled with git merge-base --is-ancestor <fix> <released commit>: exit status 1 means the released commit can't reach the fix. Nobody reads a changelog to decide it.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab. A backend team ships release builds from tagged commits. A fix for a retry bug is merged, and a customer on the previous release still sees the bug. "Is the fix in what we shipped?" is settled with `git merge-base --is-ancestor <fix> <released commit>`: exit status 1 means the released commit can't reach the fix. Nobody reads a changelog to decide it.

beats.text: And the textbook's rule about names in production: "Which commit is deployed?" must be answered with a commit ID. A tag is a name that isn't supposed to move. Whether it can is decided by the rules on the server, a GitHub matter that a later chapter covers.

beats.text: Q19: "Define "reachable". Why is a commit that no ref can reach still in the repository, and for how long by default?"
beats.tele: Q19: "Define "reachable". Why is a commit that no ref can reach still in the repository, and for how long by default?"

beats.text: Answer out loud. A strong answer gives the definition as a chain of links and says which links count. It separates the existence of an object from the existence of a name for it. For "how long", it names the mechanisms that keep or remove such a commit and the default periods the manual gives, and it knows that reflog entries are starting points too.

beats.text: Let's land this. You should now be able to say: each commit stores the IDs of its parents, so history is a graph walked from child to parent. Reachable means there is a chain of such links from a starting point, and history commands start from refs. A commit that no ref reaches still exists, and giving it a name makes it reachable again.
